claim: The larynx enables speech while regulating swallowing and respiration.
source: The larynx enables speech while regulating swallowing and respiration.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about larynx function.

claim: Larynx function hinges on the laryngeal epithelium which originates as part of the anterior foregut.
source: Larynx function hinges on the laryngeal epithelium which originates as part of the anterior foregut and undergoes extensive remodeling to separate from the esophagus and form vocal folds that interface with the adjacent trachea.
evidence: This is a statement based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: The laryngeal epithelium undergoes extensive remodeling to separate from the esophagus and form vocal folds that interface with the adjacent trachea.
source: Larynx function hinges on the laryngeal epithelium which originates as part of the anterior foregut and undergoes extensive remodeling to separate from the esophagus and form vocal folds that interface with the adjacent trachea.
evidence: This is a statement based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for epithelial integrity in the mouse larynx.
source: Here we find that sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for epithelial integrity in the mouse larynx as well as the anterior foregut.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing phenotypes in Shh mutants.

claim: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for epithelial integrity in the anterior foregut.
source: Here we find that sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for epithelial integrity in the mouse larynx as well as the anterior foregut.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing phenotypes in Shh mutants.

claim: During larynx-esophageal separation, low Shh expression marks specific domains of actively remodeling epithelium.
source: During larynx-esophageal separation, low Shh expression marks specific domains of actively remodeling epithelium that undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) characterized by the induction of N-Cadherin and movement of cells out of the epithelial layer.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 1 showing GFP expression patterns and N-Cadherin expression.

claim: Actively remodeling epithelium during larynx-esophageal separation undergoes an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) characterized by the induction of N-Cadherin.
source: During larynx-esophageal separation, low Shh expression marks specific domains of actively remodeling epithelium that undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) characterized by the induction of N-Cadherin and movement of cells out of the epithelial layer.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 1 showing N-Cadherin expression in remodeling regions.

claim: Actively remodeling epithelium during larynx-esophageal separation undergoes movement of cells out of the epithelial layer.
source: During larynx-esophageal separation, low Shh expression marks specific domains of actively remodeling epithelium that undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) characterized by the induction of N-Cadherin and movement of cells out of the epithelial layer.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data showing Shh-descendant cells in the mesenchyme.

claim: Shh mutants undergo an abnormal EMT throughout the anterior foregut and larynx.
source: Consistent with a role for SHH signaling in regulating this process, Shh mutants undergo an abnormal EMT throughout the anterior foregut and larynx, marked by a cadherin switch, movement out of the epithelial layer and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figures 2 and 3 showing cadherin switching, cell extrusion, and cell death in Shh mutants.

claim: Abnormal EMT in Shh mutants is marked by a cadherin switch.
source: Consistent with a role for SHH signaling in regulating this process, Shh mutants undergo an abnormal EMT throughout the anterior foregut and larynx, marked by a cadherin switch, movement out of the epithelial layer and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 2 and 3 showing E-Cadherin reduction and N-Cadherin induction.

claim: Abnormal EMT in Shh mutants is marked by movement out of the epithelial layer.
source: Consistent with a role for SHH signaling in regulating this process, Shh mutants undergo an abnormal EMT throughout the anterior foregut and larynx, marked by a cadherin switch, movement out of the epithelial layer and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 2 showing cells in the lumen and Figure 4 showing TdT+ cells in the mesenchyme.

claim: Abnormal EMT in Shh mutants is marked by cell death.
source: Consistent with a role for SHH signaling in regulating this process, Shh mutants undergo an abnormal EMT throughout the anterior foregut and larynx, marked by a cadherin switch, movement out of the epithelial layer and cell death.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figure 4 showing Cleaved Caspase-3 expression and TUNEL staining.

claim: Shh mutant epithelial cells are replaced by a new population of FOXA2-negative cells.
source: Unexpectedly, Shh mutant epithelial cells are replaced by a new population of FOXA2-negative cells that likely derive from adjacent pouch tissues and form a rudimentary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by data from Figures 4 and 5 showing loss of FOXA2 and Shh-descendant cells, and the presence of Hoxb1-expressing cells.

claim: The replacement population of FOXA2-negative cells likely derives from adjacent pouch tissues.
source: Unexpectedly, Shh mutant epithelial cells are replaced by a new population of FOXA2-negative cells that likely derive from adjacent pouch tissues and form a rudimentary epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from data in Figure 5 showing Hoxb1 expression patterns suggesting fourth pharyngeal pouch contribution.

claim: The replacement population of FOXA2-negative cells forms a rudimentary epithelium.
source: Unexpectedly, Shh mutant epithelial cells are replaced by a new population of FOXA2-negative cells that likely derive from adjacent pouch tissues and form a rudimentary epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by data showing persistence of an epithelial structure in mutants despite loss of original cells.

claim: SHH signaling has a default role in maintaining epithelial identity throughout the anterior foregut.
source: We propose that SHH signaling has a default role in maintaining epithelial identity throughout the anterior foregut and that regionalized reductions in SHH trigger epithelial remodeling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing loss of epithelial markers and EMT in Shh mutants.

claim: Regionalized reductions in SHH trigger epithelial remodeling.
source: We propose that SHH signaling has a default role in maintaining epithelial identity throughout the anterior foregut and that regionalized reductions in SHH trigger epithelial remodeling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing low Shh expression in remodeling regions and EMT markers.

claim: Early loss of HH signaling results in the reduction of SOX2-expressing cells from the larynx epithelium.
source: Early loss of HH signaling results in the reduction of SOX2-expressing cells from the larynx epithelium and a failure in vocal fold closure (Lungova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 5.

claim: Early loss of HH signaling results in a failure in vocal fold closure.
source: Early loss of HH signaling results in the reduction of SOX2-expressing cells from the larynx epithelium and a failure in vocal fold closure (Lungova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: HH signaling drives the separation of the trachea and esophagus.
source: HH signaling also drives the separation of the trachea and esophagus, which are directly caudal to the larynx (Billmyre et al., 2015; Han et al., 2020; Ioannides et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2019; Kuwahara et al., 2020; Nasr et al., 2019; Que et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the HH pathway transcriptional effector GLI3 cause dramatically altered larynx morphology.
source: Mutations in the HH pathway transcriptional effector GLI3 cause dramatically altered larynx morphology and vocalization defects (Tabler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mutations in the HH pathway transcriptional effector GLI3 cause vocalization defects.
source: Mutations in the HH pathway transcriptional effector GLI3 cause dramatically altered larynx morphology and vocalization defects (Tabler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Laryngeal clefts and bifid epiglottis are phenotypes of Pallister Hall syndrome.
source: Similarly in humans, laryngeal clefts and bifid epiglottis are phenotypes of Pallister Hall syndrome which arises from truncating mutations in GLI3 (Biesecker, 1993; Böse et al., 2002; Ondrey et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: Pallister Hall syndrome arises from truncating mutations in GLI3.
source: Similarly in humans, laryngeal clefts and bifid epiglottis are phenotypes of Pallister Hall syndrome which arises from truncating mutations in GLI3 (Biesecker, 1993; Böse et al., 2002; Ondrey et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: The larynx arises from an unknown cellular origin at the base of the pharynx adjacent to the fourth pharyngeal pouches.
source: The larynx arises from an unknown cellular origin at the base of the pharynx adjacent to the fourth pharyngeal pouches (Figure 1A), and bridges the anterior-most portions of the foregut to the more posterior trachea and esophagus (Essien and Maderious, 1981; Henick, 1993; Lungova et al., 2015; Poopalasundaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1A.

claim: The larynx bridges the anterior-most portions of the foregut to the more posterior trachea and esophagus.
source: The larynx arises from an unknown cellular origin at the base of the pharynx adjacent to the fourth pharyngeal pouches (Figure 1A), and bridges the anterior-most portions of the foregut to the more posterior trachea and esophagus (Essien and Maderious, 1981; Henick, 1993; Lungova et al., 2015; Poopalasundaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and anatomical knowledge.

claim: There is reduced GFP expression at the epithelial lamina which fuses and then separates the larynx and esophagus.
source: There is reduced GFP expression at the epithelial lamina which fuses and then separates the larynx and esophagus (region 1; B, H), and the constricting esophageal opening (region 2; B) of the larynx.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and H showing GFP expression patterns.

claim: There is reduced GFP expression at the constricting esophageal opening of the larynx.
source: There is reduced GFP expression at the epithelial lamina which fuses and then separates the larynx and esophagus (region 1; B, H), and the constricting esophageal opening (region 2; B) of the larynx.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B showing GFP expression patterns.

claim: N-Cadherin is expressed within the epithelial layer both in the epithelial lamina adjacent to the infraglottic duct at the site of larynx-esophageal separation.
source: Consistent with this possibility, membranous N-Cadherin was expressed within the epithelial layer both in the epithelial lamina adjacent to the infraglottic duct at the site of larynx-esophageal separation, as well as along the lateral edges of the constricting esophagus (Figure 1C, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and E showing N-Cadherin expression.

claim: N-Cadherin is expressed along the lateral edges of the constricting esophagus.
source: Consistent with this possibility, membranous N-Cadherin was expressed within the epithelial layer both in the epithelial lamina adjacent to the infraglottic duct at the site of larynx-esophageal separation, as well as along the lateral edges of the constricting esophagus (Figure 1C, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and E showing N-Cadherin expression.

claim: There was no overall reduction in E-Cadherin protein in remodeling regions.
source: While there was no overall reduction in E-Cadherin protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I), there was an increase in punctate E-Cadherin expression in both regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H', I').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: There was an increase in punctate E-Cadherin expression in remodeling regions.
source: While there was no overall reduction in E-Cadherin protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I), there was an increase in punctate E-Cadherin expression in both regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H', I').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H' and I'.

claim: RAB-11 accumulates apically at remodeling regions.
source: This is further supported by the apical accumulation RAB-11, a marker of endosome recycling that is required for the transport of E-Cadherin as well as N-Cadherin to the apical cell surface in multiple contexts (Desclozeaux et al., 2008; Kawauchi et al., 2010; Nasr et al., 2019; Welz et al., 2014; Woichansky et al., 2016; Figure 1D, F, J, L, N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D, F, J, L, N and citations to prior work.

claim: RAB-11 is a marker of endosome recycling that is required for the transport of E-Cadherin to the apical cell surface.
source: This is further supported by the apical accumulation RAB-11, a marker of endosome recycling that is required for the transport of E-Cadherin as well as N-Cadherin to the apical cell surface in multiple contexts (Desclozeaux et al., 2008; Kawauchi et al., 2010; Nasr et al., 2019; Welz et al., 2014; Woichansky et al., 2016; Figure 1D, F, J, L, N).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RAB-11 is required for the transport of N-Cadherin to the apical cell surface.
source: This is further supported by the apical accumulation RAB-11, a marker of endosome recycling that is required for the transport of E-Cadherin as well as N-Cadherin to the apical cell surface in multiple contexts (Desclozeaux et al., 2008; Kawauchi et al., 2010; Nasr et al., 2019; Welz et al., 2014; Woichansky et al., 2016; Figure 1D, F, J, L, N).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There were a small number of RFP-labeled cells within the mesenchyme along the anterior–posterior axis of the separating larynx and esophagus.
source: Consistent with prior reports using a related ShhCre strategy (Lungova et al., 2018), there were a small number of RFP-labeled cells within the mesenchyme along the anterior–posterior axis of the separating larynx and esophagus (Figure 1P, Q).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1P and Q and citation to prior work.

claim: There was no significant increase in the number of mesenchymal RFP-labeled cells at later stages of larynx-esophageal separation.
source: While there was a significant increase in the domain of N-Cadherin expression within the remodeling epithelium at later stages of larynx-esophageal separation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), there was no significant increase in the number of mesenchymal RFP-labeled cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Some Shh-descendant cells undergo EMT-based extrusion during larynx remodeling but they do not remain in the mesenchyme.
source: This suggests that some Shh-descendant cells undergo EMT-based extrusion during larynx remodeling but they do not remain in the mesenchyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing limited numbers of mesenchymal cells despite N-Cadherin expression.

claim: EMT was the most significantly enriched pathway among HH-dependent genes.
source: Consistent with our model, EMT was the most significantly enriched pathway among HH-dependent genes (Figure 2A), supporting a role for HH signaling in regulating this process.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in Shh mutants consisted of members of all three progressive EMT stages.
source: Differentially expressed genes consisted of members of all three progressive EMT stages (Figure 2B; Lamouille et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior work defining EMT stages.

claim: Dsp and Dcn are downregulated in Shh mutants, marking the first stage of EMT.
source: These included downregulation of the pro-epithelial adhesion genes Dsp, and Dcn, which mark the first stage (Bax et al., 2011; Huang et al., 2012; Kowalczyk and Nanes, 2012; Wang et al., 2015; Yilmaz and Christofori, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior work.

claim: Cdh2, Vimentin, and Fn1 are upregulated in Shh mutants, indicative of the next phase of EMT.
source: There was also an upregulation of the pro-migratory genes Cdh2, Vimentin, and Fn1, indicative of the next phase of EMT (Wheelock et al., 2008; Yilmaz and Christofori, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior work.

claim: Lama1 is downregulated in Shh mutants, suggestive of a breakdown in the basement membrane which is one indicator of the third stage of EMT.
source: Finally, there was a downregulation of Lama1, which encodes for Laminin, suggestive of a breakdown in the basement membrane which is one indicator of the third stage of EMT (Aumailley and Smyth, 1998; Lamouille et al., 2014; Nakaya et al., 2008; Thiery and Chopin, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior work.

claim: Several TGFβ family members were upregulated in Shh mutants.
source: In addition, several TGFβ family members were upregulated, suggesting a plausible mechanism for inducing EMT (Barrallo-Gimeno and Nieto, 2005; Katsuno et al., 2013; Mercado-Pimentel and Runyan, 2007; Nawshad et al., 2004; Schnaper et al., 2003; Thiery et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior work on TGFβ's role in EMT.

claim: N-Cadherin (Cdh2) was highly upregulated within the mutant epithelium.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data and evocative of the observations in remodeling epithelia (Figure 1), N-Cadherin (Cdh2) was highly upregulated within the mutant epithelium along with substantial reduction of pro-epithelial E-Cadherin (Cdh1) and p63 (Figure 2C–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: E-Cadherin (Cdh1) was substantially reduced in the mutant epithelium.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data and evocative of the observations in remodeling epithelia (Figure 1), N-Cadherin (Cdh2) was highly upregulated within the mutant epithelium along with substantial reduction of pro-epithelial E-Cadherin (Cdh1) and p63 (Figure 2C–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: p63 was substantially reduced in the mutant epithelium.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq data and evocative of the observations in remodeling epithelia (Figure 1), N-Cadherin (Cdh2) was highly upregulated within the mutant epithelium along with substantial reduction of pro-epithelial E-Cadherin (Cdh1) and p63 (Figure 2C–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Loss of epithelial stratification was accompanied by a shift in the adhesive properties of the larynx epithelium toward a mesenchymal profile.
source: This suggested that loss of epithelial stratification was accompanied by a shift in the adhesive properties of the larynx epithelium toward a mesenchymal profile.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing loss of E-Cadherin and p63 and gain of N-Cadherin.

claim: Laminin was lost from the basement membrane along the epithelium in Shh mutants.
source: This change was further accompanied by a loss of Laminin from the basement membrane along the epithelium (Figure 2B, G, H) indicating that HH signaling is required to maintain the integrity of this structure.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: HH signaling is required to maintain the integrity of the basement membrane.
source: This change was further accompanied by a loss of Laminin from the basement membrane along the epithelium (Figure 2B, G, H) indicating that HH signaling is required to maintain the integrity of this structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing loss of Laminin in Shh mutants.

claim: Col4a2 and Nid2 were upregulated in Shh mutants.
source: Additional basement membrane component genes such as Col4a2 and Nid2 were upregulated by RNA-seq, suggesting that loss of Laminin may result in a compensatory increase in other basement membrane components in order to maintain membrane integrity (Jones et al., 2016; Salmivirta et al., 2002; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Loss of Laminin may result in a compensatory increase in other basement membrane components to maintain membrane integrity.
source: Additional basement membrane component genes such as Col4a2 and Nid2 were upregulated by RNA-seq, suggesting that loss of Laminin may result in a compensatory increase in other basement membrane components in order to maintain membrane integrity (Jones et al., 2016; Salmivirta et al., 2002; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is speculated based on the data showing upregulation of other basement membrane components and citations to prior work.

claim: Single cells appeared to be extruding from the epithelial layer into the lumen in Shh mutants.
source: Interestingly, single cells appeared to be extruding from the epithelial layer into the lumen (Figure 2I–I") and clusters of cells were present within the lumen of the epithelium (Figure 2J, J').
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2I-I".

claim: Clusters of cells were present within the lumen of the epithelium in Shh mutants.
source: Interestingly, single cells appeared to be extruding from the epithelial layer into the lumen (Figure 2I–I") and clusters of cells were present within the lumen of the epithelium (Figure 2J, J').
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2J, J'.

claim: Luminal cell clusters were first seen at E10.5 and increased dramatically by E11.5.
source: These clusters were first seen at E10.5 and increased dramatically by E11.5 (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: There was a reduction in the levels of E-Cadherin in the Shh−/− epithelium of the presumptive larynx as early as E9.5.
source: To determine the onset of this phenotype, we examined earlier stages of foregut development and found a reduction in the levels of E-Cadherin in the Shh−/− epithelium of the presumptive larynx as early as E9.5 (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Membranous N-Cadherin was first observed in a small number of cells within the epithelial layer at E9.5 and at E9.75.
source: Although N-Cadherin was not initially expressed at high levels, expression of membranous N-Cadherin was first observed in a small number of cells within the epithelial layer at E9.5 and at E9.75 (Figure 3C, D, N).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C-D and quantification in Figure 3N.

claim: E-Cadherin re-localized within cells, moving from high expression along the lateral cell boundaries to accumulating in puncta along the apical surface.
source: Over the next few hours of development E-Cadherin re-localized within cells, moving from high expression along the lateral cell boundaries to accumulating in puncta along the apical surface (Figure 3E–G), but was maintained in the epithelium as late as E10.0 (Figure 3J, K; Aiello et al., 2018; Woichansky et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E-G and citations to prior work.

claim: More than half of the cells within the epithelium expressed robust levels of membranous N-Cadherin at E10.0.
source: At this stage, more than half of the cells within the epithelium expressed robust levels of membranous N-Cadherin (Figure 3L–N) suggesting that N-Cadherin is induced in cells simultaneously expressing E-Cadherin at this stage.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3L-N.

claim: N-Cadherin is induced in cells simultaneously expressing E-Cadherin during EMT.
source: At this stage, more than half of the cells within the epithelium expressed robust levels of membranous N-Cadherin (Figure 3L–N) suggesting that N-Cadherin is induced in cells simultaneously expressing E-Cadherin at this stage. This is consistent with recent studies that have described coexpression of E-Cadherin and N-Cadherin in cells undergoing EMT (Aiello et al., 2018; Ray and Niswander, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: E-Cadherin and N-Cadherin appeared to be coexpressed within a small number of TdT-expressing epithelial cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75.
source: While E-Cadherin and N-Cadherin had mutually exclusive boundaries restricted to the epithelium and mesenchyme, respectively, in controls, they appeared to be coexpressed within a small number of TdT-expressing epithelial cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 (Figure 3P–Q; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, D).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3P-Q.

claim: Laryngeal epithelial cells undergo a cadherin switch in the absence of HH signaling.
source: Coexpression was also observed at E10.0, both as distinct apical puncta and laterally along cell–cell boundaries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), indicating that laryngeal epithelial cells undergo a cadherin switch in the absence of HH signaling.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The switch in cadherin expression within the vocal folds occurred on the transcriptional level with Cdh1 expression replaced by high levels of Cdh2 expression by E10.5.
source: The switch in cadherin expression within the vocal folds also occurred on the transcriptional level with Cdh1 expression in the mutant epithelium at E9.25 replaced by high levels of Cdh2 expression by E10.5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: There was an increase in low-level Vimentin expression along the apical surface of TdT-expressing epithelial cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 compared to controls.
source: As suggested by the transcriptional increase in pro-migratory factors at E10.5, there was an increase in low-level Vimentin expression along the apical surface of TdT-expressing epithelial cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–B, B1–B1", E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B, E.

claim: Vimentin expression marked a small number of TdT-expressing cells within the mesenchyme in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75.
source: Vimentin expression also marked a small number of TdT-expressing cells within the mesenchyme in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at this stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B2–B2"; 4/12 mesenchymal TdT+ cells).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B2-B2" and quantification.

claim: SNAIL expression was not detected within the mutant epithelium.
source: SNAIL expression was not detected within the mutant epithelium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D, D1–D1''', E) but approximately half of the TdT-expressing epithelial cells in the mesenchyme were also positive for SNAIL expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D2'–D2'''; 5/9 mesenchymal TdT+ cells) suggesting that TdT+ cells that migrate into the mesenchyme are capable of transiently expressing mesenchymal cell markers (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C-D, E.

claim: Approximately half of the TdT-expressing epithelial cells in the mesenchyme were positive for SNAIL expression.
source: SNAIL expression was not detected within the mutant epithelium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D, D1–D1''', E) but approximately half of the TdT-expressing epithelial cells in the mesenchyme were also positive for SNAIL expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D2'–D2'''; 5/9 mesenchymal TdT+ cells) suggesting that TdT+ cells that migrate into the mesenchyme are capable of transiently expressing mesenchymal cell markers (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D2'-D2''' and quantification.

claim: TdT+ cells that migrate into the mesenchyme are capable of transiently expressing mesenchymal cell markers.
source: SNAIL expression was not detected within the mutant epithelium (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C–D, D1–D1''', E) but approximately half of the TdT-expressing epithelial cells in the mesenchyme were also positive for SNAIL expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D2'–D2'''; 5/9 mesenchymal TdT+ cells) suggesting that TdT+ cells that migrate into the mesenchyme are capable of transiently expressing mesenchymal cell markers (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing SNAIL expression in mesenchymal TdT+ cells.

claim: FOXA2 activates the expression of Cdh1 and suppresses EMT programs in the endoderm.
source: FOXA2 activates the expression of Cdh1 and suppresses EMT programs in the endoderm (Bow et al., 2020; Scheibner et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: FOXA2 was expressed in nearly every cell at the region of the future larynx in both control and Shh−/−s during early stages of foregut development (E9.25).
source: Consistent with this scenario, FOXA2 was expressed in nearly every cell at the region of the future larynx in both control and Shh−/−s during early stages of foregut development (E9.25; 21–23 somites; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: By E9.75, FOXA2 expression was not detectable in ~30–40% of the mutant cells with reduced expression in many of the remaining FOXA2+ cells.
source: However, by E9.75 (27–29 somites), FOXA2 expression was not detectable in ~30–40% of the mutant cells with reduced expression in many of the remaining FOXA2+ cells (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: FOXA2 was further reduced by E10.5 and completely absent by E11.5 in Shh mutants while expression remained robust in controls.
source: FOXA2 was further reduced by E10.5 and completely absent by E11.5 while expression remained robust in controls (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–J).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G-J.

claim: There was Ptch1 and low-level Gli1 expression within the larynx epithelium.
source: In keeping with the latter possibility, there was Ptch1 and low-level Gli1 expression within the larynx epithelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that HH signaling could potentially regulate FOXA2 through autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: HH signaling could potentially regulate FOXA2 through autocrine signaling.
source: In keeping with the latter possibility, there was Ptch1 and low-level Gli1 expression within the larynx epithelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), indicating that HH signaling could potentially regulate FOXA2 through autocrine signaling.
evidence: This is speculated based on the data showing HH pathway activity in the epithelium.

claim: FOXA2 was not downregulated at the site of larynx-esophageal separation or along the lateral edges of the constricting esophagus in wild-type embryos.
source: In contrast to the early foregut (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), FOXA2 was not downregulated at the site of larynx-esophageal separation or along the lateral edges of the constricting esophagus (Figure 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–F3, G, H, I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-I.

claim: FOXA2 regulation by HH signaling is specific to early stages of foregut and larynx development.
source: We conclude that FOXA2 regulation by HH signaling is specific to early stages of foregut and larynx development.
evidence: This is concluded based on the differential FOXA2 expression patterns at different stages.

claim: There was an increase in the number of labeled cells within the adjacent mesenchyme surrounding the epithelium in mutant embryos at E9.75–E10.5.
source: Consistent with earlier experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), there was an increase in the number of labeled cells within the adjacent mesenchyme surrounding the epithelium in mutant embryos (E9.75–E10.5, Figure 4H, I, K, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D, E, Supplementary file 1) suggesting EMT induction.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4H-I, K and Figure 4—figure supplement 4D-E.

claim: The low number of mesenchymal cells suggested that most of the cells leaving the epithelium do not survive.
source: The low number of these cells suggested that most of the cells leaving the epithelium do not survive.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantification of mesenchymal cells.

claim: There were high levels of cell death in both the mesenchymal and epithelial tissues of the vocal folds between E9.5 and E11.5, peaking at over 30% of the epithelium.
source: Consistent with this idea, there were high levels of cell death in both the mesenchymal and epithelial tissues of the vocal folds between E9.5 and E11.5, peaking at over 30% of the epithelium (Figure 4H, J; Figure 4—figure supplement 5A–H).
evidence: This is supported by TUNEL and Cleaved Caspase-3 data shown in Figure 4H, J and Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-H.

claim: Mesenchymal TdT-expressing cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 did not express the apoptosis marker Cleaved Caspase-3.
source: Initially, mesenchymal TdT-expressing cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 did not express the apoptosis marker Cleaved Caspase-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4F, F', Supplementary file 1) however by E10.5, the majority of ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+-labeled cells outside the epithelium were apoptotic (Figure 4H, J, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4F, F'.

claim: By E10.5, the majority of ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+-labeled cells outside the epithelium were apoptotic.
source: Initially, mesenchymal TdT-expressing cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+s at E9.75 did not express the apoptosis marker Cleaved Caspase-3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4F, F', Supplementary file 1) however by E10.5, the majority of ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+-labeled cells outside the epithelium were apoptotic (Figure 4H, J, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H, J.

claim: Most of the vocal fold cells undergoing EMT in Shh−/− embryos are either in the process of undergoing apoptosis or undergo apoptosis shortly after extrusion.
source: We conclude that most of the vocal fold cells undergoing EMT in Shh−/− embryos are either in the process of undergoing apoptosis or undergo apoptosis shortly after extrusion.
evidence: This is concluded based on the data showing high levels of apoptosis in extruded cells.

claim: During the initial period of cell death, proliferation levels remained unchanged.
source: During the initial period of cell death, proliferation levels remained unchanged. However, by E11.5 there was a significant increase in cell proliferation within the vocal fold epithelium of Shh−/− embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 5I–J).
evidence: This is supported by pHH3 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5I-J.

claim: By E11.5 there was a significant increase in cell proliferation within the vocal fold epithelium of Shh−/− embryos.
source: During the initial period of cell death, proliferation levels remained unchanged. However, by E11.5 there was a significant increase in cell proliferation within the vocal fold epithelium of Shh−/− embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 5I–J).
evidence: This is supported by pHH3 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5I-J.

claim: The Shh−/− epithelium was highly disorganized with highly variable epithelia containing increased numbers of cell layers (an average of 12 layers).
source: Notably, the Shh−/− epithelium was highly disorganized. Compared to the uniform, one to two cell layers observed in control embryos, mutant embryos had highly variable epithelia containing increased numbers of cell layers (an average of 12 layers; Figure 4—figure supplement 6A–C), with an overall thickening of the vocal fold epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6A-C.

claim: The aberrant epithelium continued to persist until at least E13.5, and was composed of rudimentary, poorly keratinized, p63-negative cells that did not recover normal epithelial form or function.
source: This aberrant epithelium continued to persist until at least E13.5, and was composed of rudimentary, poorly keratinized, p63-negative cells that did not recover normal epithelial form or function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Shh descendants were primarily localized to the ventral half of the vocal fold epithelium by E10.5.
source: Using the same ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+ embryos described above, we found that Shh descendants were primarily localized to the ventral half of the vocal fold epithelium by E10.5 (Figure 4D–F, L), mirroring previous reports of ventral Shh expression in the early foregut (Burke and Oliver, 2002; Moore-Scott and Manley, 2005; Motoyama et al., 1998; Rankin et al., 2016; Sagai et al., 2009; Szabó et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4D-F, L and citations to prior work.

claim: There was a sharp decrease in Shh-descendant cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+ mutants.
source: In marked contrast to control embryos, there was a sharp decrease in Shh-descendant cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+ mutants (Figure 4H, J, L), indicating that the aberrant epithelium observed at later stages was not descended from the initial epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4H, J, L.

claim: The aberrant epithelium observed at later stages was not descended from the initial epithelium.
source: In marked contrast to control embryos, there was a sharp decrease in Shh-descendant cells in ShhCreER/−;Rosa26Ai9/+ mutants (Figure 4H, J, L), indicating that the aberrant epithelium observed at later stages was not descended from the initial epithelium.
evidence: This is inferred from the lineage tracing data showing loss of Shh-descendant cells.

claim: At E10.5 there is an absence of NKX2.1 in Shh mutants.
source: At E10.5 there is an absence of NKX2.1 and a significant reduction in nuclear SOX2, which is undetectable by E11.5 (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: At E10.5 there is a significant reduction in nuclear SOX2 in Shh mutants, which is undetectable by E11.5.
source: At E10.5 there is an absence of NKX2.1 and a significant reduction in nuclear SOX2, which is undetectable by E11.5 (Figure 5A–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Larynx epithelial cells are abnormally patterned in Shh−/− embryos.
source: We conclude that larynx epithelial cells are abnormally patterned in Shh−/− embryos.
evidence: This is concluded based on the loss of SOX2 and NKX2.1 expression.

claim: Pax1 was expressed exclusively in pharyngeal pouches 1–3 and was excluded from the epithelium and mesenchyme of the vocal folds in controls.
source: Consistent with previous findings, Pax1 was expressed exclusively in pharyngeal pouches 1–3 and was excluded from the epithelium and mesenchyme of the vocal folds in controls (Figure 5F, H–J, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A; Johansson et al., 2015; Moore-Scott and Manley, 2005; Westerlund, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5F, H-J and citations to prior work.

claim: Hoxb1 was highly expressed in the fourth pharyngeal pouches adjacent to the larynx and was also transiently expressed at lower levels within the epithelium of the vocal folds at E10.5.
source: Hoxb1, which was highly expressed in the fourth pharyngeal pouches adjacent to the larynx was also transiently expressed at lower levels within the epithelium of the vocal folds at E10.5, defining it as a marker of the larynx in control and mutant tissues at this timepoint (Figure 5F, G, J, Figure 4—figure supplement 6A", B" 1–2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5F-J and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The fourth pharyngeal pouches were contracted toward the larynx in mutants at E10.0, forming a single continuous structure with the same high Hoxb1 expression along the lateral walls in anterior sections through the larynx.
source: At 30–32 s (E10.0), just prior to widespread cell death within the epithelium, Shh−/− embryos had severely altered pharyngeal pouch and larynx morphology. The fourth pharyngeal pouches were contracted toward the larynx in mutants, forming a single continuous structure with the same high Hoxb1 expression along the lateral walls in anterior sections through the larynx, which resolved into separated pouch and foregut epithelia posteriorly (Figure 5P–Q).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5P-Q.

claim: Pax1 and Hoxb1 domains remained unchanged in Shh−/− embryos at both E10.75 and E11.5 while FOXA2 was either severely reduced or absent from the larynx and anterior foregut.
source: Despite these severe morphology changes, Pax1 and Hoxb1 domains remained unchanged in Shh−/− embryos at both E10.75 (37–38 s) and E11.5 (42–44 s) while FOXA2 was either severely reduced or absent from the larynx and anterior foregut (Figure 5F–Q, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, D–F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5F-Q and Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2.

claim: Foxn1, which marks the third pharyngeal pouch, did not expand into the larynx in Shh mutants.
source: Similarly, Foxn1, which marks the third pharyngeal pouch, did not expand into the larynx (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–D; Moore-Scott and Manley, 2005; Wallin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-D and citations to prior work.

claim: The abnormally positioned fourth pharyngeal pouches fuse with and replace part of the larynx epithelium in Shh−/− embryos while more anterior pouch tissues do not expand into the larynx.
source: This suggests that the abnormally positioned fourth pharyngeal pouches fuse with and replace part of the larynx epithelium in Shh−/− embryos while more anterior pouch tissues do not expand into the larynx.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Hoxb1 expression patterns and lack of Pax1/Foxn1 expansion.

claim: The liver bud is generated from foregut tissue that lacks Shh expression and subsequently undergoes EMT into the adjacent mesenchyme.
source: The liver bud is generated from foregut tissue that lacks Shh expression and subsequently undergoes EMT into the adjacent mesenchyme (Bort et al., 2006; Mu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of Shh and the expression of N-Cadherin within the foregut epithelium mark the site of the presumptive dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds.
source: Additionally, loss of Shh and the expression of N-Cadherin within the foregut epithelium mark the site of the presumptive dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds, though N-Cadherin is dispensable for the initial stages of pancreatic budding (Esni et al., 2001; Johansson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: N-Cadherin is dispensable for the initial stages of pancreatic budding.
source: Additionally, loss of Shh and the expression of N-Cadherin within the foregut epithelium mark the site of the presumptive dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds, though N-Cadherin is dispensable for the initial stages of pancreatic budding (Esni et al., 2001; Johansson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hhex mutants, which fail to undergo EMT of the liver bud, mis-express Shh in the epithelium.
source: While the role of Shh has not been directly studied in this process, Hhex mutants, which fail to undergo EMT of the liver bud also mis-express Shh in the epithelium (Bort et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.
